scenario.speaker: marcus
scenario.briefing:
We won it. Dana signed the **Neo Smart Living** engagement this morning — secondary research, focus groups, and a survey over fourteen weeks. It's the largest project on the board, and phase one starts with you.

Phase one is **secondary research**. Neo needs to know three things before we spend a dollar on primary data: who the Tahoe Mini actually competes against, which features the market is rewarding, and where the price benchmarks sit. I've pulled three recent industry pieces — they're attached to my memo in your **Inbox**, and they contain everything you need if you read them like an analyst instead of like a magazine subscriber.

One warning up front: the coverage spans **two different product categories** — finished backyard studios like the Tahoe Mini, and expandable tiny homes with kitchens and bathrooms, which is where Neo's *other* product, the Mojave, competes. Keep the line straight; this engagement is about the Tahoe Mini.

Your three assignments: identify the **competitive set**, recommend the **feature priorities**, and extract the **price benchmarks**. The **Guides** button has my method for pulling findings out of secondary sources without drowning in them. Extraction, not summary — Dana reads the output of this round in Friday's client call.

inbox.subject: We got Neo — phase one is yours
inbox.body:
First things first: your proposal work paid off. Neo Smart Living signed this morning — all three phases, fourteen weeks. Dana actually smiled in a meeting, which the old-timers tell me happens once a fiscal year.

Now the bill comes due. Phase one is secondary research, and the client call is Friday, so we move today. I've pulled three industry pieces covering the backyard-structure market — they're attached below. Together they hold the answers to the three questions Neo is paying us for this phase:

1. **Competitive set.** Eight companies show up in the coverage, but they split across two categories: finished backyard studios with no plumbing — the Tahoe Mini's market — and expandable container homes with kitchens and bathrooms, which is ADU territory and the market for Neo's own **Mojave**. Four companies belong on the Tahoe Mini's benchmark list. Work out which four — and don't let a tempting price tag drag a different product category onto the list.
2. **Feature priorities.** The buyer-trends and forecast pieces tell you what the market rewards and what it punishes. Turn that into a recommended specification, category by category.
3. **Price benchmarks.** Advertised prices in this market are not comparable numbers — some buy a shell, some a finished unit, some a turnkey installed project. Extract the closest competitor's advertised price, and the pair of numbers from the kit segment that shows exactly how far a headline price can sit from an installed one. Those are the rulers we'll use all project long.

Read all three pieces before you answer anything; they check each other. And mind the category line — benchmarking a $23,000 studio against a plumbed 400-square-foot dwelling is the kind of mistake that follows an analyst around.

— Marcus

attachments.title: Backyard Studios, Space Pods, and Expandable Tiny Homes: A Category Field Guide
attachments.body:
*Structure & Site Quarterly — annual category review*

The fastest-growing corner of factory-built housing is also the easiest to misread, because two genuinely different products share the same backyard. This review covers both — and the legal line between them.

**The line is the ADU definition.** In California, an accessory dwelling unit must provide complete independent living facilities: living, sleeping, eating, cooking, and sanitation (Government Code § 66313). An ADU is a *legal land-use classification*, not a manufacturer's label — a factory-built unit becomes one only when its installation, utilities, and permits satisfy the local jurisdiction. A **backyard studio or space pod** deliberately stays on the other side of that line: no plumbing, no kitchen, a non-habitable accessory structure that in many cases avoids building permits entirely. An **expandable container tiny home** ships compact, unfolds on site, and — because it carries a kitchen and bathroom — is ADU-*capable*, with the permits, foundations, and utility connections that capability implies.

**Category one: finished studios and pods.** The reference product here is the **Autonomous WorkPod**, a 102-square-foot backyard office pod advertised at **$20,900** in its DIY configuration. Insulation comes standard, the unit sits on adjustable foundation feet, power arrives through a single-cable connection, and the company publishes inventory, delivery estimates, and customer reviews for direct online purchase. **Studio Home's Signature Series** takes the customization route: 96 to 192 square feet, advertised from about **$18,000**, with a configurator offering broad choices of openings, colors, and interior packages — installation and interiors priced separately through a nationwide network. **Modern Shed** goes further bespoke: consultant-led design intended to match the primary residence, California installer support (though it does not employ installers directly), and no public price list — quotes only. At the kit end, **Kanga Room Systems** sells its Modern Kwik Room 10×12 — 120 square feet, an almost exact size match for the units above — as a nationwide shell kit at **$18,900**; in Texas, and only in Texas, the same room can be bought as a **$24,700** installed shell or a **$40,600** turnkey build. The gap between Kanga's headline and its turnkey number is the category's standing lesson: foundation, electrical, insulation, flooring, and finish carry real prices whether or not the advertisement mentions them. Among newer entrants, Southern California's **Neo Smart Living** sells the glass-forward, 117-square-foot **Tahoe Mini** — advertised from **$19,800**, and typically **$23,000 delivered and installed** including tax and warranty, supported by a Chino showroom.

**Category two: expandable homes and foldable ADUs.** **Bright Box Homes** anchors this market with expandable container homes from **$35,995** (200–800 square feet) that ship with a mini-split, tankless water heater, and induction stove as standard — utilities and permits remain the buyer's problem, and the units are marketed as temporary buildings. **Symmetry's PF-208** offers roughly 430 square feet at **$38,700** basic or **$51,600** with an engineering package, and is unusually transparent about delivery, setup, and foundation add-ons. **Elite Nest** advertises a 400-square-foot expandable home from **$16,999**, described as 95% complete with a finished kitchen and bathroom — a headline that has pulled search traffic from studio shoppers, though engineering documentation, delivery, installation, permits, and warranty scope are far less transparent than the price. At the premium end, **BOXABL's Casita** — the category's most famous name — runs about **$60,000** unit-only, or roughly **$150,000** in its California turnkey program, with factory-installed kitchen, bathroom, HVAC, and the most complete documentation in the field.

**Substitutes press both categories.** A contractor-finished shed kit or a garage conversion competes with every studio pod on structural cost; a certified travel trailer such as the **ESCAPE Vista Boho** (about 187 square feet, **$57,640**, RVIA-certified) competes with expandable homes on mobility and financing; and a conventional site-built ADU remains the permanent-housing alternative.

**The analyst's rule.** Buyers cross-shop within a category, not across the backyard as a whole. A $16,999 expandable dwelling is not a cheap studio, and a $20,900 office pod is not an expensive shed — they answer different customer jobs under different laws. Sort first; compare second.

attachments.title: Backyard-Unit Buyer Trends by Homeowner Segment
attachments.body:
*Home & Yard Business Journal — buyer-trends brief*

Who actually buys a finished backyard unit, and what do they want from it once it lands? Retailer interviews and two waves of syndicated purchase-tracking data point to three homeowner segments with distinct — and occasionally conflicting — demands.

**The remote professional** accounts for roughly forty-five percent of tracked purchases, and this buyer wants an office, not a room. Purchase drivers are consistent: separation from the household, daylight ("I refuse to work in a garage cave," one buyer told our researchers), and a desk-ready interior — work surface, shelving, task lighting — rather than an empty shell they must furnish themselves. Yet the same glass-forward designs that win this buyer at purchase generate the category's two most common post-purchase complaints: afternoon heat gain and the sensation of "working on display" in view of neighboring second-story windows. Demand has shifted accordingly toward dual-pane glazing with a privacy option — switchable film, integral blinds, or solid-panel swaps — rather than either fully glazed or nearly windowless designs.

**The wellness user** — roughly thirty percent of purchases and the fastest-growing segment — wants a yoga, meditation, or small-fitness studio. This buyer asks about resilient or sprung flooring, a mirror wall, air movement, and, more than any other segment, privacy. Retailers report wellness buyers walking away from all-glass showroom units after a single question: "Can the neighbors see in?"

**The guest-space buyer** rounds out the category at roughly a quarter of purchases and is softening: interest cools quickly once shoppers learn that unplumbed, non-habitable structures cannot legally or practically serve as true guest quarters. The buyers who persist migrate out of the studio category entirely — into expandable, ADU-capable units with kitchens and bathrooms, at two to three times the outlay and a very different permitting journey.

Two demands now cut across all three segments. First, climate comfort has become a threshold expectation rather than an upgrade: buyers in the hotter inland and Sun Belt metros increasingly treat insulation plus a mini-split heating-and-cooling unit as the minimum for year-round use, and units marketed with fans-only ventilation are drawing elevated complaint and return rates. Second, buyers rarely ask about smart-home extras unprompted, but they expect the basics handled on day one: powered outlets installed by a professional and a door that locks.

attachments.title: Opportunities & Forecasts for the North American Compact-Structure Market
attachments.body:
*Compact Structures Outlook — five-year category forecast*

Forecasters expect the compact accessory-structure category to grow at roughly eleven percent annually through 2030, with the persistence of remote and hybrid work as the primary demand engine and permit-light formats — units sized under local permitting thresholds — as the primary supply-side accelerant. Growth is projected to concentrate in Sun Belt and West Coast metros, where year-round outdoor usability and high housing costs make a finished backyard room an attractive alternative to moving. The finished-studio segment is projected to capture the majority of that growth; shell kits grow in units but not much in dollars, and the expandable-ADU segment remains constrained by permitting timelines.

**Feature outlook.** Synthesizing buyer surveys, dealer interviews, and warranty-claim data, our analysts project the five attributes buyers will most demand over the forecast window:

1. **Insulated composite panel construction** — the single strongest predictor of owner satisfaction in claims and review data
2. **Dual-pane glazing with a privacy option** — resolving the category's signature heat-and-exposure complaints without giving up daylight
3. **A full climate package** — insulation plus mini-split heating and cooling, increasingly expected as standard
4. **Work-from-home interior fit-out** — desk, shelving, and lighting delivered ready to use
5. **Pre-wired electrical with smart entry lock** — professional power on day one, with security handled quietly in the background

On materials, the same data carries warnings: single-skin steel and untreated timber kits are losing share on durability and comfort complaints, and while premium hardwood cladding tests well aesthetically, few buyers in this category will pay its increment — it wins compliments, not orders. Unfinished shells continue to disappoint owners who underestimate finishing costs.

**Pricing outlook.** Advertised prices for finished studios in the 100-to-120-square-foot class now cluster between $18,000 and $21,000: Autonomous WorkPod at $20,900 with insulation standard, Studio Home from about $18,000 before installation and interiors, Kanga's Modern Kwik Room at $18,900 — for a shell. And that last word is the analysts' central warning: **advertised prices are not comparable across completion levels.** Kanga's own Texas program reprices the $18,900 shell at $40,600 turnkey — a $21,700 gap representing foundation, electrical, insulation, flooring, finish, and labor that every buyer pays somewhere, whether or not the advertisement mentions it. The comparison that decides a purchase is *total cost to a legally usable, climate-appropriate, installed space*. Sellers who advertise a delivered-and-installed price should say so loudly: an installed $23,000 can be cheaper in practice than an advertised $18,900. New entrants are advised to publish completion levels explicitly and compete on specification — headline-price limbo against shell kits is a race the finished-studio segment cannot win and should not enter.

guides.title: Round 4 — Reading Secondary Research Without Drowning
guides.body:
**Extraction beats summary.** A summary tells your boss what an article said; an extraction answers the client's question. Before you read a word, write down the table you intend to fill — then read only to fill it.

**Make three passes, one per question:**

1. **Competitor grid.** For every company named: product category, size, price, and its one-line claim to fame. Then apply the definition that matters: a *competitor* is a company your buyer would cross-shop — not every company with a backyard SKU. Sort by category before you compare anything: a finished studio with no plumbing and an expandable dwelling with a kitchen answer different customer jobs under different laws.
2. **Feature signals.** Collect what buyers *praise*, what they *complain about after purchase* (the strongest signal in secondary data — it's behavior, not opinion), and what forecasters *rank*. When a complaint and a forecast point at the same feature, that's your headline.
3. **Price benchmarks.** Pull every price into one table *with its completion level* — shell kit, finished unit, turnkey installed. Comparisons are only meaningful within a completion level; a shell and a turnkey are different products wearing the same dollar sign, and one mismatched number in your benchmark can move a recommendation by tens of thousands.

**Triangulate.** A finding in one source is a claim; the same finding in two independent sources is a finding; in three, it's a plan. When sources disagree, recency and independence break the tie.

**Check recency and credibility.** Note each piece's publication cadence and vantage point. An advertised price is a marketing document, not a project budget — fine for positioning a brand, risky for estimating what a buyer actually pays. Trade-press analysis beats vendor-sponsored content; data with a described method beats data without one.

**Pointers for this round:** keep the two product categories separate before comparing anything — a tempting price in the wrong category is the classic trap; when a headline price looks like an outlier, check its completion level before drawing any conclusion; and read all three articles before answering, because the feature questions are answered across two of them, not one.
